query: For high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could improve dynamic strength–ductility performance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an untreated baseline, defines the boundary conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of interstitial elements, such as oxygen or nitrogen, to high-entropy alloys can improve their dynamic strength-ductility performance by enhancing solid solution strengthening and forming ordered interstitial complexes.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a single-phase BCC structure
generation.intervention: Addition of interstitial elements, such as oxygen or nitrogen
generation.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening and formation of ordered interstitial complexes, derived from materials-science principles and partially supported by records PMC11077685, PMC10759803, and PMC7299626
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved dynamic strength-ductility performance, with a predicted increase in yield strength of 10-20% and elongation of 5-10%
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 300-1100 K and strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of improvement in dynamic strength-ductility performance may vary depending on the specific composition and processing route of the high-entropy alloy

falsification_experiment.design: Compression testing and damping measurements on high-entropy alloys with and without interstitial elements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of interstitial elements does not result in a significant improvement in dynamic strength-ductility performance, the hypothesis is falsified.

System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Question: How can equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy be synthesized into complex shapes via additive manufacturing, and how can its oxidation resistance be improved for extreme temperature applications?. System: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) synthesized from a blend of hydride powders (TiH2, ZrH2, HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5) and elemental powders. Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
